name: G10 FX carry trade
heading: The Structural Opportunity: Earning Interest Rate Differentials
caseLead: Higher-yielding currencies have historically fallen by less than their interest rate advantage would imply, allowing carry investors to earn the difference when exchange rates remain relatively stable. The premium persists because central banks set rates for domestic inflation and growth rather than for exchange rate returns, while investors who need stable funding or safe assets accept low returns in the yen and Swiss franc, and policy divergence between the Federal Reserve, the Reserve Bank of Australia and the Bank of Japan keeps the gap open.
caseRest: The strategy typically earns modest carry returns but can suffer sharp losses when investors reduce risk. In these episodes, high-yielding currencies fall while funding currencies such as the yen and Swiss franc rise, so the strategy loses on both sides of the trade within days. A strong risk-adjusted return can therefore understate the downside risk, as the losses coincide with falls in equity markets and are hard to avoid by selling beforehand.
figNote: The large figure on each card shows the level of USD/JPY, the number of yen needed to buy one US dollar, at its high or low during the episode. A higher figure means a weaker yen, which favours investors who hold higher-yielding currencies funded in yen.

events.title: Lehman collapse forces a global carry unwind
events.text: The failure of Lehman Brothers in September 2008 forced investors to repay yen borrowing, so USD/JPY fell to about 91 in October. The strategy lost because high-yielding currencies such as the Australian dollar fell sharply as positions were closed.

events.title: Bank of Japan surprises with more easing
events.text: The Bank of Japan's surprise easing on 31 October 2014, combined with the end of Federal Reserve bond purchases, lifted USD/JPY to about 122 by early December. The strategy gained because the widening rate gap favoured holding higher-yielding currencies against the yen.

events.title: Brexit vote sends investors into the yen
events.text: The June 2016 vote to leave the European Union pushed USD/JPY to about 99 as investors bought the yen and sold sterling. Results were mixed because the strategy lost on the day but regained part of the loss as markets stabilised.

events.title: Covid sets off a global rush for dollars
events.text: The March 2020 spread of Covid-19 drove USD/JPY to about 101 as US yields collapsed, then a global rush for dollars hit commodity currencies. The strategy lost because the Australian, New Zealand and Norwegian currencies fell sharply against both the dollar and the yen.

events.title: Fed rate rises widen the gap with Japan
events.text: A widening gap between the Federal Reserve's rate rises and the Bank of Japan's negative policy rate lifted USD/JPY to about 152 in October 2022. The strategy gained on the rate gap, although Japanese intervention caused sharp but brief reversals.

events.title: Yen surges as funded positions are closed
events.text: A Bank of Japan rate rise on 31 July 2024 and weak US jobs data pushed USD/JPY from about 162 in July to 142 on 5 August. The strategy lost because positions funded in yen were closed within days.

instrument: G10 currency forwards; one to three months to expiry; rolled monthly
rules: Long the three highest-yielding currencies and short the three lowest-yielding, ranked by three-month interest rate; sized by volatility; put options bought on the long basket
costs: Estimated bid-ask spreads and forward points deducted at each roll
constructionTitle: Strategy construction, from interest rate differentials to loss limits

legs.purpose: Funds the long positions at low rates

legs.position: Put options on the long basket
legs.purpose: Limits losses in a sudden fall in risk appetite
Provides collateral and earns the cash rate

entry: Interest rate gap of at least 2 percentage points between long and short currencies
size: Set to an 8% annualised volatility target
exit: Positions rebalanced monthly, or closed when the rate ranking changes
stop: Exposure halved if the VIX closes above 30
marketWatch: G10 interest rate differentials, central bank decisions and implied currency volatility are the key indicators for this strategy. Rehyn tracks the Federal Reserve, the Bank of Japan and the Reserve Bank of Australia because changes in expected policy rates alter the gap that the strategy earns. Upcoming central bank meetings and warnings of intervention in the yen matter most because they can reverse positions within days.

favourable.heading: Stable policy rate differences
favourable.text: Persistent gaps between policy rates favour the strategy because it earns the differential each month while exchange rates change little. A widening gap between US and Japanese rates supported returns in 2014 and again in 2022.

favourable.heading: Low currency volatility
favourable.text: Low implied volatility favours the strategy because exchange rates move by less than the rate gap over a month, so most of the differential is kept. This was the pattern in 2017, when currency volatility stayed close to record lows and higher-yielding currencies gained steadily.

favourable.heading: Regional tension stays contained
favourable.text: Regional tension favours the strategy when it does not change global risk appetite, because funding currencies do not rally. After Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, higher energy prices lifted the Norwegian and Canadian currencies while the yen weakened as US yields rose.

adverse.heading: Sudden global risk aversion
adverse.text: A sharp fall in risk appetite hurts the strategy because investors buy funding currencies and sell high-yielding ones at the same time. In March 2020, the Australian dollar fell by more than 15% against the US dollar within weeks as the dollar rose against most G10 currencies.

adverse.heading: Central bank action in funding countries
adverse.text: A rate rise or intervention in a funding-currency country hurts the strategy because it raises the cost of borrowing in that currency and prompts positions to close together. The Bank of Japan's rate rise in July 2024 helped lift the yen by about 12% against the US dollar in five weeks.

adverse.heading: Narrowing policy rate gaps
adverse.text: A narrowing of rate gaps hurts the strategy because it reduces the income earned and removes the reason to hold the higher-yielding currency. In March 2020, the central banks of Australia and New Zealand cut rates to 0.25%, removing most of the yield advantage over the yen and Swiss franc.

infoHist: Historical results show the strategy's peak-to-trough drawdown during each event, measured from its value just before the event to its lowest point using the default backtest parameters above. Each event window runs from the last market high before the shock to the market low.
infoForward: Scenario results show the estimated profit or loss over the first month of each scenario. Rehyn's scenario engine projects moves in G10 exchange rates, interest rate differentials and implied currency volatility, which are then applied to the strategy's current positions, including the protective options.

related.why: Holds currencies below fair value for years. Bears slow convergence, losing when they move further from it.
related.cue: Pays for valuation, not interest rates
